description_ru: Эссе-возражение против культа эффективности: почему жизнь, из которой убрали всё лишнее, перестаёт быть жизнью.
text:
A friend of mine, a man of considerable intelligence and diminishing hair, recently confessed to me that he had optimised his mornings. He rises at 5:42, never 5:45, because an application informed him that this was the moment at which his sleep cycle was most obliging. He consumes a beverage made of powdered nutrients, so as to save the eleven minutes that a boiled egg would have cost him, and listens to a podcast at double speed, so that a book on the history of the Roman Empire can be absorbed during his shave. When I asked whether he enjoyed any of this, he looked at me with genuine bewilderment. Enjoyment, it seemed, was not among the metrics.

Our age has fallen in love with a word. To optimise is, in its original sense, to make the best of something, and there is nothing sinister in that. A good engineer optimises a bridge; a sensible cook optimises the use of a pan. But the verb has escaped from the workshop and wandered into the drawing room, the bedroom and the nursery, where it has set about reorganising everything we do into a series of problems with measurable solutions. We now optimise our diets, our friendships, our holidays, our children and, with a solemnity worthy of a funeral, our leisure. The result is a civilisation of the perpetually improved, and, curiously, of the perpetually dissatisfied.

The trouble begins with a logical sleight of hand. To optimise anything, one must first decide what is being maximised, and this requires a number. Happiness cannot be tallied, but steps can, and so we count steps. Friendship is elusive, but followers can be counted, and so we count followers. A good evening is a delicate mixture of wine, conversation and accident, but an hour of productivity can be measured, and so it is measured, and gradually becomes the only thing that matters. The economist's maxim that what gets measured gets managed is not a recommendation; it is a warning that we neglect to read.

There is an old tale about a king who loved his horse so dearly that he ordered it to be fed on the finest barley, in strict measures, three times a day. The horse thrived for a week, and then, quite unreasonably, declined. A groom, in a moment of daring, suggested that the animal might like to wander in the meadow. Everything that made the horse a horse, its caprice, its appetite for the unplanned mouthful of clover, had been optimised away. I confess that I invented this story, but I suspect that it is true in every respect that matters.

Consider what is lost when efficiency becomes an ideology. The long, unhurried walk to the shop, which could have been a delivery, was also the occasion on which you met your neighbour, noticed the lime tree in blossom and thought of something to say to your sister. The meandering dinner party, which a ruthless accountant would condemn as a colossal squandering of hours, is the soil in which friendships and conspiracies are planted. Serendipity, that most precious of accidents, is by definition inefficient. It lives in the margins of the schedule, and the optimiser, with his tidy diary, has abolished the margins.

I do not wish to be unfair to the optimisers, who are, after all, motivated by a perfectly decent anxiety. Time is finite, and the thought of its being wasted is painful. Yet the logic is self-defeating, since the minutes saved are never spent on anything particularly valuable. They are promptly reinvested in further optimisation, in a spiral resembling a hamster's wheel that has been fitted with a dashboard. The man who saves eleven minutes at breakfast usually discovers that he has acquired a fresh obligation to fill them. The great myth of the labour-saving device is that it saves labour; what it saves is merely the pretext for more of it.

Nor does the philosophy of optimisation survive close examination on its own terms. A truly optimised life would require perfect knowledge of the future, since only then can one say that one chose the best course. We possess nothing of the kind. We are creatures who stumble along in the fog, guessing; and the bold theory that we can eliminate error by tracking enough data is the most recent in a long line of fantasies, from alchemy to central planning, in which the muddle of the world is to be replaced by a tidy mechanism. The muddle, as ever, declines to cooperate.

What I propose, therefore, is a modest rebellion in favour of the sufficient. The economist Herbert Simon coined the word satisficing for the habit of choosing an option that is good enough, rather than agonising over the best, and he observed that those who satisfice tend to be happier than those who maximise. They are not less ambitious; they are merely less haunted. They order from the menu in thirty seconds, leave the restaurant without wondering whether the place next door was superior, and have spare attention to devote to the conversation, which is, after all, why they came.

It is perhaps worth adding that nothing of value in my own life has ever been the result of an optimal decision. I met my wife because a train was delayed. I found my profession because a more sensible one rejected me. My best friend was assigned to me as a flatmate by an administrative error, and my favourite city is one I reached by taking the wrong bus. If these accidents were to be audited by a productivity consultant, he would recommend their immediate elimination, and my life would be considerably better organised and almost entirely empty.

I therefore invite you to practise a little deliberate inefficiency. Take the longer road. Cook something that takes too long. Read a book slowly, even rereading a paragraph for no reason except its beauty. Allow a free afternoon to remain free, and resist the urge to populate it with improvements. Wasting time, I am increasingly convinced, is not a vice but a skill, and perhaps the last true luxury in an age that has made everything else cheap. As for my friend, I am happy to report that last week he missed his alarm, overslept until seven and, by his own account, had the most delightful breakfast of his life.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Нижняя губа касается верхних зубов, голос включён; не заменяйте на «ф» и не на губное «w».
Губы вытянуты вперёд, зубов не касаются; произносите коротко, без русского «в».
Кончик языка не касается нёба, а губы чуть округлены; не раскатывайте русское «р».
Короткий, открытый, округлый звук: не растягивайте и не заменяйте русским «а».

questions.question: Why does the author's friend wake at 5:42?
questions.answer: An application told him that was the best moment for his sleep cycle.

questions.question: What does the author call the habit of choosing what is good enough?
What is the story about the king's horse meant to show?
questions.answer: Over-optimising removes what makes life natural and alive.

questions.question: How does the author's friend end up?
questions.answer: He overslept and had the best breakfast of his life.
